what.text: Estriol is an estrogen, a female sex hormone. It is one of the natural estrogens the body makes.
FDA labeling for estrogens says estradiol is the main estrogen inside cells and is substantially more potent than its breakdown products, estrone and estriol, at the estrogen receptor.

In some European countries estriol is a prescription vaginal cream for postmenopausal women with vaginal dryness and irritation (vaginal atrophy). Absorption into the blood from that cream is described as very low.

src.label: HPRA (Ireland), Ovestin 1 mg per gram vaginal cream, licence record

what.text: Adonis's catalog lists estriol in two face creams: estriol 0.03% with tretinoin 0.1% (30 g), and estriol 0.3% with niacinamide 3% and GHK-Cu 0.2% (15 to 45 g). Whether these are compounded or approved products is still being confirmed.
Estriol is a hormone. Using it on a man’s skin is off-label: it is not an approved use anywhere we checked.

research.text: Human evidence on estriol for skin aging: two small studies from one Vienna group in the 1990s, both in women around menopause, both comparing estriol cream with estradiol cream. We found no study of estriol on men’s skin and no placebo-controlled trial.
Each is listed below as it was run.

research.title: Facial skin aging, pilot, 1994 (Austria)

facts.v: pilot study comparing two creams. No placebo group.
18 perimenopausal women: 8 used 0.3% estriol cream, 10 used 0.01% estradiol cream on the face
skin aging signs at monthly dermatology visits, blood hormone levels, and gynecological and breast checks

research.found: Both groups showed improvement in skin aging signs. The authors reported the estriol group was slightly better in extent and onset. No hormonal side effects were noted. The authors advised limiting strength and area of application to reduce the risk of whole-body hormone effects.

research.title: Skin aging, two estrogen creams, 1996 (Austria)

facts.v: comparison of 0.01% estradiol and 0.3% estriol creams. The abstract does not describe a placebo group or randomization.
59 preclimacteric women with skin aging signs; skin biopsies in 10
skin firmness and elasticity, wrinkle depth by profilometry, skin moisture, collagen in biopsies, blood hormone levels

research.found: Wrinkle depth fell significantly in both groups, skin moisture rose, and biopsies showed more type III collagen. Prolactin rose significantly; no systemic hormonal side effects were noted.

src.label: Schmidt et al., Int J Dermatol, 1996

research.text: Both studies were in women. Their results cannot be assumed to apply to men.

items.text: estriol or plain cream on the backs of male and female rats for two weeks. In females, collagen fibrils thickened and the fat layer under the skin thinned; skin stiffness rose in both sexes, and breaking and tensile strength fell in females. The changes differed between male and female rats.

src.label: Ozyazgan et al., Med Sci Monit, 2005

items.lead: Mice and a population study, China, 2025:
items.text: estriol was found in 73 of 240 skincare cosmetics bought in China. Mice given estriol creams on the skin had higher thyroid antibodies. In people, a cross-sectional study found no difference in thyroid antibodies between cosmetic users and non-users, but a case-control study linked cosmetic use with autoimmune thyroid disease (odds ratio 1.577). The authors call this preliminary.

us.text: There is no FDA-approved estriol product in the US. Estriol medicines sold in the US are compounded and not FDA-approved. As of October 31, 2026.

items.text: none. FDA says there are no FDA-approved drugs containing estriol, and that marketed estriol drugs are compounded drugs, which are not FDA-approved.
FDA says it does not have evidence that drugs containing estriol are safe and effective, or are “safer forms of estrogen.”

a National Academies review requested by FDA found a lack of rigorous evidence of safety and effectiveness for compounded bioidentical hormone therapy, and concluded its widespread use poses a public health concern.

items.text: FDA lists estriol in Category 1 (under evaluation). It is not marked as a component of an FDA-approved drug.

items.text: estriol does not appear in FDA’s 503A nominations categories. Under the law, a 503A pharmacy may use a bulk substance that meets a USP monograph, is a component of an approved drug, or is on FDA’s 503A list.

us.text: Whether the estriol products Adonis carries are compounded or approved is still being confirmed. No estriol product is FDA approved in the US, so a compounded one would not be FDA approved either. Any use on men’s skin is off-label.
Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.

world.lead: Estriol is not approved in the US or Canada. In Ireland, an EU country, an estriol vaginal cream is a licensed prescription medicine for postmenopausal vaginal atrophy. No regulator we checked approves estriol for skin aging or for use in men.

countries.status: Not approved. Compounded only; on FDA’s 503B list under evaluation.

after.text: Estriol is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List. Estrogens themselves are not a prohibited class; section S4 bans aromatase inhibitors and anti-estrogenic substances, which block estrogen. The 2027 list, in force January 1, 2027, does not change this.

src.label: WADA 2027 List, summary of modifications and explanatory notes

side.text: Estriol is an estrogen. In men, estrogens can cause breast changes and other hormone effects. There is no estriol label written for men, so the points below come from estrogen labels and from the studies above.

items.text: breast tenderness, enlargement and pain; nipple discharge; changes in libido; fluid retention (edema); nausea; headache; blood clots in veins; stroke; and skin darkening (melasma). The label does not give rates for men.
FDA labeling says large doses of estrogen, like those once used for prostate cancer, raised the risk of nonfatal heart attack, pulmonary embolism and thrombophlebitis in a large trial in men.

for an estradiol skin spray, FDA labeling reports breast budding in young girls and gynecomastia (breast growth) and breast masses in young boys after accidental contact with the treated skin. This was reported for estradiol, not estriol.

the Irish leaflet lists breast swelling and tenderness, minor vaginal bleeding, discharge, painful urination, nausea, fluid retention, local irritation or itching and flu-like symptoms. It notes HRT risks such as blood clots and stroke apply less to vaginal products.
neither 1990s study noted hormonal side effects; prolactin rose in the 1996 study.

src.label: Schmidt et al., Int J Dermatol, 1996

items.text: one Chinese study linked estriol-containing cosmetics with thyroid antibodies in mice and with autoimmune thyroid disease in a case-control study.

unconfirmed: FDA's January 2008 action on compounded estriol (warning letters to pharmacies over “bioidentical” hormone claims) could not be confirmed: FDA's archived press release could not be opened, so it is left out.
We could not confirm whether a USP monograph for estriol exists, which affects whether 503A pharmacies may compound it.
Approval of estriol vaginal cream was confirmed only in Ireland (a parallel-import licence); other EU countries were not checked one by one.
Status in the UK and Australia was not checked against a regulator record.
A 2026 systematic review of topical estrogen for skin aging (J Am Acad Dermatol) has no abstract we could open, so its findings are not reported.
We found no published study of estriol applied to men's skin.
Whether the product Adonis carries is compounded or an FDA-approved product is still being confirmed.
surprises: Estriol is often marketed as a weaker or “safer” estrogen; FDA says it has no evidence that estriol drugs are safe and effective or are safer forms of estrogen, and that no FDA-approved estriol drug exists.
In Ireland estriol is a licensed prescription vaginal cream for women, while in the US every estriol product is compounded and unapproved.
All skin-aging studies we found were in women around menopause; none were in men, the group this page is for.
